A user asking for the cause of a failure wants a diagnosis, not a choice with rationale; 'what are my options' style requests are distinct from 'why did this fail'. No shared trigger scope.

Debug diagnoses a concrete failure (code/test/lint/runtime/CI); architect produces system structure from design drivers. A failure-cause request has no structural-design deliverable, so no normal debug request reasonably triggers architect.

A request inside debug's scope asks for a diagnosis (the cause of a failure), which plan explicitly excludes ('diagnosing failures (debug)'). Plan's scope is producing an ordered implementation sequence; wanting the cause does not reasonably trigger plan, and plan's exclusion of diagnosis removes the overlap despite the 'plan the fix' phrasing.

The descriptions draw a clean boundary: debug handles diagnosing unknown failures, build handles implementing fixes with a known cause. A request like 'why is this test failing' routes to debug, while 'fix this bug (known cause)' routes to build. Neither description's positive scope captures the other's core case, and both explicitly exclude each other.
A user asking for the cause of a failure wants a diagnosis, not a pre-merge review; review's scope (readiness, simplification, quality of a diff) doesn't reasonably cover 'why did this fail'.

Both descriptions explicitly carve out the other's scope: debug excludes Git command failures and repository-state questions, while git-ops excludes diagnosing why code/tests/CI failed even after a Git operation. A request like 'why did my tests fail after the rebase' lands unambiguously in debug, and 'fix this checkout error' lands in git-ops. The overlap in trigger context (Git operations) is shared vocabulary, not a routing collision.

A request like 'should I rebase or merge this branch?' is squarely inside git-ops's positive scope (rebases, merges) while also matching decide's 'should I' / options-with-rationale pattern; neither description's exclusions exclude it.

Git operations and repository-state questions have no overlap with system-structure design requests; a normal Git request (commits, branches, conflicts) would not reasonably trigger the architect route.

Git/GitHub requests (commits, branches, conflicts, errors) are repository-state operations, not requests for an ordered implementation sequence. Plan's scope (breakdown, ordering, scoping work) doesn't reasonably trigger from a normal git query, and plan explicitly excludes diagnosing/debugging, which is where git-adjacent confusion would land.

Git operations requests (commits, branches, rebases, history) stay within git-ops and don't imply writing or fixing code. Build targets implementation/bug-fix requests, and git-ops explicitly excludes failure diagnosis, so a normal git request wouldn't reasonably trigger build.

A user asking about a pull request or merge (e.g., 'is this PR ready to merge?', 'check this diff before I merge') falls squarely in git-ops' positive scope (pull requests, merges) while also matching review's explicit triggers ('is this ready to merge', 'check this diff'). Neither description's exclusions prevent the overlap: git-ops only excludes failure diagnosis, and review imposes no git-related exclusion.

The boundary is explicitly drawn both ways: git-ops covers Git command/checkout errors and repository-state questions, while debug covers diagnosing code/test/lint/runtime/CI failures and explicitly excludes Git command failures and repository-state questions. A request clearly inside git-ops's positive scope (e.g., a checkout error or missing commits) is a Git command/repo-state issue that debug's description excludes, so no normal git-ops request reasonably triggers debug.
